messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Restrained): Feeling physically restrained or held down, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Vignette:
Mateo, a 37-year-old social ministry worker, had never imagined that the man he loved could become a source of terror. The night it happened, they had been arguing—about money, about his late hours at the parish, about everything and nothing. His partner had been drinking; the sickly sweet smell of whisky filled the small apartment. When Mateo tried to walk away, a hand grabbed his wrist and yanked him back. He was shoved onto the bed, and then a heavy knee pressed into his chest, pinning him down. He could not move, could barely breathe. Somewhere in the chaos, the bedroom door slammed hard against the frame, and the sound seemed to echo for hours. That was the last time he ever entered that apartment. In the weeks that followed, he packed his things while a friend stood guard, and he never went back.

Mateo’s work kept him moving between the church office, a food pantry, and the homes of families he tried to support. But the world had become a place full of hidden threats. At the pantry, a volunteer once clapped him on the shoulder from behind, and Mateo’s entire body locked—arms rigid, breath stopped—as if he were being held down again. The volunteer laughed and said he was jumpy; Mateo forced a smile, but his heart hammered for the rest of the shift. He learned to stand with his back to the wall at all times, scanning for any sudden movement. The sound of a door slamming in the parish hall would send a jolt through him, and he would flinch before he could stop himself. He started arriving early to meetings just to ensure he could sit where no one could approach from behind.

The hardest moments came during home visits. Some families lived in neighborhoods where the smell of alcohol drifted from open windows, and Mateo’s stomach would clench. He found himself making excuses to avoid certain streets, rerouting his drives even if it meant being late. At night, his vigilance grew unbearable. He checked every lock in his apartment twice, three times, before he could try to sleep. When memories surfaced—and they did, vividly, with sounds that seemed to come from the room around him—he heard the slam of that door, the scrape of a shoe on the floor, the ragged breathing. A wave of grief would wash over him, not just for the relationship he had lost but for the sense of safety he would never recover.

He tried to keep his emotions under tight control. At work, he smiled and nodded through conversations, but behind his calm face he was constantly scanning, always braced. A colleague once remarked that Mateo seemed “closed off,” and he shrugged it off with a half-hearted joke. But he knew the truth: he was afraid that if he let even one feeling slip, the wall he had built would crumble and he would freeze in the middle of the day, unable to move. At thirty-seven, he had spent years building a career helping others, and the thought of that identity crumbling terrified him more than the memories themselves.

What finally brought him to therapy was a minor incident that became a major one. Last week, during a home visit to a single mother, the woman’s young son ran into the room unexpectedly. Mateo did not have time to react—he froze completely, his face blank, his hands trembling. The mother asked if he was okay, and he could only nod, unable to speak. He left early, drove home shaking, and spent that night checking the locks until his fingers were sore. The next morning, he called the parish counselor and made an appointment. He did not know if talking could truly help. But he was exhausted. He wanted to stop feeling like a prisoner in his own body. He wanted to visit a home without wondering who might grab him, and he wanted to hear a door close without flinching. He was terrified that if he did not find a way to let go of this constant guard, he would lose the one thing he still had: his ability to help others.
